newsitem.title: KENYA: Tough African stance on Burundi mystifies some.
newsitem.headline: Tough African stance on Burundi mystifies some.

text.p: The "blunt instrument" style of diplomacy adopted by African leaders on the Burundi crisis has started to alarm some diplomats and mediators.
So far none is willing to publicly voice the concerns about the uncompromising policy nor openly criticise Julius Nyerere, the elder statesman believed to be its driving force.
But in private they are mystified by the refusal to make any concession to Burundi's military government and fear it will lead to explosive failure.
"To resolve any conflict you need to show the parties both a carrot and a stick. What we are seeing on Burundi is all stick and no carrot," said an experienced foreign mediator.
"This approach is not building any trust between the Hutus and the Tutsis," he told Reuters this week in Bujumbura, the frightened capital.

Burundi's suicidal slide into the abyss has accelerated quickly. But its lack of strategic importance has meant the world's great powers are unwilling to intervene directly to separate warring communities as they did in ex-Yugoslavia.
They devolved the task of finding a solution to Africa and chiefly to Nyerere, the former Tanzanian president who became the international and foreign-funded "facilitator" for Burundi last February.
His efforts to get the two sides talking and persuade the Tutsi minority to share power were rebuffed last July 25 when the overwhelmingly Tutsi army staged a coup.
Six days later regional countries imposed a total trade and transport embargo, the first time that Africa, on its own, has used the sanctions weapon.
Nyerere has not visited Burundi since the coup. He is demonised by Tutsis who say he has a pro-Hutu secret agenda.
"He probably wouldn't survive a visit if he came here now. But you can't mediate if one side won't talk to you," a Western diplomat in Burundi said.
Breakdown came last Saturday when a regional summit maintained the sanctions and ordered military President Pierre Buyoya to enter talks with Hutu rebels within a month.
The decision ignored the urgings of U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to give Buyoya some breathing space.
Within 48 hours Burundi called the bluff -- no talks until sanctions are lifted -- and panicky depression gripped Bujumbura for a few hours.
"That's it, I'm taking my family to Rwanda to start from scratch. It will be total war now," said a Tutsi businessman.
Like many Tutsis, some Hutus and more than a few diplomats and mediators, he believes Buyoya is a relative moderate who could strike a deal with the rebels.

"Buyoya has virtually met the letter, if not the spirit, of the three conditions the leaders gave at the outset," one diplomat said. These were the unbanning of political parties, the restoration of parliament and the start of negotiations with armed factions.
Those talks have not begun but Buyoya, in writing, is committed to them.
"They should have eased the sanctions. They have given Buyoya no room for manoeuvre at all," a diplomat said.
"Now both sides have painted themselves into corners. There is a total impasse."

It may be that Nyerere and the pro-sanctions hardliners, Kenya and Tanzania, disbelieve Buyoya's coded warnings that he will be toppled by Tutsi colonels if he enters talks without any prior concessions.
Or they may feel that come what may the same colonels will never accept power-sharing with a Hutu majority they fear will exterminate them.
In that case the stage is set for total war and the progressive dismemberment of Burundi into ethnic zones.
